pages.x: Bohdan Khmelnytsky was a Cossack officer in Ukraine, then part of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. In 1647 a Polish nobleman seized his estate, carried off the woman he loved and had his son flogged, and the courts gave him no justice. He fled to the Cossacks of the Zaporozhian Sich, beyond the Dnieper rapids, and called them to war.

With Crimean Tatar horsemen as allies, the Cossacks destroyed two Polish armies in May 1648: at Zhovti Vody, the Yellow Waters, and at Korsun, where both Polish commanders were captured. Peasants across Ukraine rose against their lords, and the rebels swept west toward Lviv.

The rising brought terrible massacres. Rebels killed Polish nobles, Catholic priests and above all Jews, whom they saw as the lords' agents. Thousands of Jews died in towns like Nemyriv and Tulchyn, and Jewish chroniclers remembered it as one of the great catastrophes of their history. Polish troops answered with massacres of their own.

Beaten at Berestechko in 1651 when his Tatar allies fled, Khmelnytsky looked for a stronger protector. In January 1654, at Pereiaslav, the Cossack officers swore loyalty to Tsar Alexis of Russia, who shared their Orthodox faith. That summer Russian armies invaded the Commonwealth. They took Smolensk that autumn, and Minsk and Vilnius in 1655.

In July 1655 King Charles X Gustav of Sweden invaded from the north and west. Polish nobles went over to him almost without a fight, Warsaw and Kraków fell, and King John Casimir fled to Silesia. With Russians, Cossacks and Swedes all inside the country, Poles came to call these years the Deluge.

A few places held out. At Częstochowa the monks and soldiers of the monastery of Jasna Góra, home of a famous icon of the Virgin Mary, beat off a Swedish siege for about forty days at the end of 1655. Poles took it as a miracle, and it turned a lost war into a crusade against Lutheran invaders.

John Casimir came back at the start of 1656. In the cathedral of Lviv he placed his kingdom under the protection of the Virgin Mary, naming her Queen of Poland, and promised to ease the burdens of the peasants once peace came. Stefan Czarniecki led a guerrilla war that wore the Swedes down, and the country rose behind them.

Czarniecki even followed the Swedes to Denmark in 1658, and swam his horses across the sea to the island of Als. Poland's national anthem, written in 1797 when the country had been wiped off the map, still sings of him coming home across the sea to save his homeland.

Sweden's enemies multiplied, and after Charles X Gustav died, the Peace of Oliva in 1660 ended the Swedish war. The war with Russia dragged on until the Truce of Andrusovo in 1667 split Ukraine along the Dnieper. Russia kept Smolensk and the lands east of the river, and Kyiv, which was meant to be handed back after two years and never was.

Two centuries later, when Poland had been divided up by its neighbours, Henryk Sienkiewicz wrote a great novel about the Swedish war, The Deluge, to lift the hearts of his people. Read by generations of Poles and filmed in 1974, it gave the wars the name most Poles know them by.

The Commonwealth survived, but it lost perhaps a third of its people to war, hunger and plague, and it never recovered its strength. In the 1700s its neighbours divided it up. In Ukraine, Khmelnytsky is honoured as the founder of a Cossack state, and Russia, holding Kyiv, became eastern Europe's rising power.
